lesson.title: Logical Fallacies
lesson.summary: The most common reasoning errors and how to identify them in arguments — and in your own thinking.

blocks.text: A logical fallacy is an error in reasoning that makes an argument invalid, even if it seems convincing. Recognizing fallacies is essential for critical thinking.

items: Ad hominem: attacking the person instead of the argument
Straw man: distorting the opponent's position to refute it more easily
Appeal to authority: accepting something as true because an authority said so
False dichotomy: presenting only two options when more exist

blocks.text: An argument that sounds good is not always a good argument.
Fallacies appear in political speeches, advertising, public debates, and everyday conversations. Identifying them protects you from manipulation and improves the quality of your own arguments.

cards.front: What is the ad hominem fallacy?
cards.back: Attacking the character or circumstances of the person making the argument, rather than responding to the argument itself.

cards.front: What is the straw man fallacy?
cards.back: Distorting or exaggerating the opponent's position to refute it more easily, rather than attacking the actual argument.
Presenting a situation as if only two opposite options exist, when in reality more alternatives are available.

quiz.question: Which of the following is an example of ad hominem?
options: Your proposal doesn't work because it ignores factor X
Don't listen to him — he was never a good student
This solution is too expensive to implement
The data shows a different result than expected
quiz.explanation: Ad hominem attacks the person (never a good student) instead of responding to the argument being made.

quiz.question: What is the problem with the straw man fallacy?
options: It uses false data to support an argument
It refutes a distorted version of the original argument
It appeals to emotions instead of reason
It uses authority to validate an idea
quiz.explanation: The straw man creates an easier-to-refute version of the opponent's argument, avoiding the actual debate.
